name: Caroni Swamp
blurb: Mangroves, fiddler crabs and the scarlet ibis roost on Trinidad's west coast.

tip.title: Remove the fiddler crabs
tip.text: Crabs feed ibises, herons, raccoons and caimans. Set Fiddler crabs to -100% and watch the wading birds and predators that rely on them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Tropical sun drives growth of the mangroves and of the algae on the mudflats.

nodes.name: Freshwater inflow
nodes.desc: The Caroni River meets the Gulf of Paria here, mixing fresh and salt water and carrying silt and nutrients into the swamp.

nodes.name: Tides and brackish water
nodes.desc: Tides flood the channels and lagoons twice a day, setting the salinity that mangroves tolerate and moving crabs, fish and larvae in and out.

nodes.name: Nutrient-rich mud
nodes.desc: Intertidal mud and mangrove peat hold nutrients and feed the algae and crabs living on the flats.

nodes.name: Red mangrove
nodes.desc: Prop-rooted tree on the water edge. Its thickets give nesting and hunting habitat for fish, birds and crabs, and ibises roost in young waterside mangroves.

nodes.name: Black mangrove
nodes.desc: Mangrove of the higher, saltier mud, forming part of the forest that makes Caroni the largest mangrove stand on the island.

nodes.name: White mangrove
nodes.desc: Mangrove of the drier landward fringe, one of three mangrove trees recorded around the swamp.

nodes.name: Mudflat algae
nodes.desc: Microscopic algae and diatoms on the intertidal mud, the base of the food for grazing crabs, fish and insect larvae.

nodes.name: Green iguana
nodes.desc: Large leaf-eating lizard that climbs in trees and is recorded eating mangrove foliage.

nodes.name: Fiddler crabs
nodes.desc: Burrowing crabs that sift mud for algae, microbes and detritus, and are a main food for wading birds and other predators here.

nodes.name: Four-eyed fish
nodes.desc: Surface-dwelling fish of the brackish waters of the swamp, with eyes adapted to look above and below the water.

nodes.name: Salt-marsh mosquito
nodes.desc: A mosquito whose larvae develop in brackish water; its larvae and adults are prey for fish and insect-eating bats.

nodes.name: Trinidad tree boa
nodes.desc: Tree-climbing snake reported in the swamp. GloBI records it eating green iguanas.

nodes.name: Scarlet ibis
nodes.desc: The swamp is the largest roost for this bird, which feeds on crustaceans, small fish, molluscs and insects; its red colour comes from the shellfish it eats.

nodes.name: Little blue heron
nodes.desc: A wading heron that hunts by sight for fish and crabs; in some mangroves crabs make up most of its diet.

nodes.name: Crab-eating raccoon
nodes.desc: Omnivore of marshy places in Trinidad that eats crabs, shellfish, fish, amphibians and fruit.

nodes.name: Proboscis bat
nodes.desc: Small insectivorous bat that roosts on waterside trunks and feeds on flying insects such as mosquitoes.

nodes.name: Black vulture
nodes.desc: Common scavenger that eats dead animals around the wetland, including lizards and birds in GloBI records.

nodes.name: Spectacled caiman
nodes.desc: Caiman of calm waters in Trinidad and Tobago; adults take fish, crabs and snails, birds and mammals.

nodes.name: Osprey
nodes.desc: Fish-eating raptor commonly recorded over the swamp.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Bacteria, fungi and mud-dwelling invertebrates break down fallen mangrove leaves and wood and return nutrients to the mud.
